title: Space Management
summary: Space organisation means assigning space to an activity and arranging systematically all the materials needed for it: allotting space, making all that is required available on the spot and arranging materials and equipment. It saves time and energy. Functional storage means storing the things for a task near where the task is done. Two activities done near each other can be dovetailed, for example washing utensils while food is cooking when water is in the kitchen, or cutting vegetables while watching TV. When space is limited, rooms are used for more than one purpose: a bedroom as a study during the day and a living room as a bedroom at night.

Household activities are cooking, washing clothes and utensils, sleeping, studying, playing and watching TV, and entertaining; each can be split into sub-activities (cooking: storing, pre-preparation, cooking, washing utensils, serving and storing left-overs). The area specified for an activity is a work centre; it does not need a separate room, and similar activities can share one room.

Cooking area: things used often are kept at a convenient height, heavy and frequently used containers (atta, rice) at floor level, and rarely used things in high places, called dead storage. Kitchen layouts: one-walled, two-walled (parallel), L-shaped and U-shaped; also sitting or standing kitchen. A folding dining table fixed on the wall saves space; the utensil washing area should be near the cooking area. Bathing area: storage for soaps, powders and toiletries, proper water supply and drainage, a sloping, non-slippery floor, electrical points away from water, space for a washing machine and soiled clothes and a clothesline near the washing area. Sleeping area: pull-out and trunk beds, bunk beds, folding beds, beds with drawers (preferably on wheels), side tables, a wall-fixed mirror instead of a dressing table, a built-in almirah up to the ceiling and a study table. Study area: good natural and artificial light, least disturbance, bookshelf along the wall. Entertainment area: drawing room divided into sitting and dining parts, a divider with shelves, sofa-cum-bed, diwan and folding beds. A one-room house must fit all work centres in one room, distinguishing the areas.

Guidelines for effective work centres: arrange in a sequential order (pre-preparation, washing, cooking, serving), use transparent or labelled storage containers, give adequate lighting and ventilation, make centres easy to clean, prefer built-in storage to cupboards, and create storage under the staircase, below window slabs and in lofts. Aesthetics: furniture to suit room size (small and light in a small room), an organised look, arrangement that does not hinder movement, furniture arranged by activity, good lighting (a well-lit small room looks spacious), distinguishing areas in a one-room flat, light colours and a white ceiling for dark small rooms, and decorative items and indoor plants.

objective: Fill in the blanks. (a) Work centres should be arranged in a ________ order to assist in the smooth flow of work. (b) Storage bins should be ________ so that contents can be seen.
Fill in the blanks. (a) All work centres in the kitchen should have adequate ________. (b) To save floor space, cupboards should be replaced with ________ storage.

vsa: What two essential provisions each would you ensure in a kitchen and a bathroom?
Kitchen: a convenient height for storage and a source of water with a washing area. Bathroom: a non-slippery sloping floor with drainage, and electrical points away from water.
Why is it important to arrange things in an orderly manner at home?
It saves time and energy in finding things and looks neat and attractive. It also gives a feeling of more space and makes cleaning easy.
The area specified for an activity at home is a work centre. It need not be a separate room; similar activities can share one room.
Differentiate between functional storage and dead storage.
Functional storage keeps the things for a task near the place of the task. Dead storage keeps rarely used things in less accessible high places.
List any two ways of saving space in a bedroom.
Use pull-out or bunk beds and beds with drawers for storage. Fix a mirror on the wall instead of a dressing table and build the almirah into the wall.
sa: Explain space organisation and its significance (three points).

(i) It is assigning space to an activity and arranging all the required materials systematically. (ii) It saves time and energy because everything is available on the spot. (iii) It makes effective use of limited space, such as the living room being used for sleeping at night.
List the guidelines for making a work centre more effective.

(i) Arrange work centres in a sequential order and have transparent or labelled containers. (ii) Provide adequate lighting and ventilation and keep centres easy to clean. (iii) Prefer built-in storage and use space under the staircase, window slabs and lofts.
How can aesthetics be created in a work area? (three points)

(i) Furniture of suitable size and an organised look. (ii) Good lighting and light colours that make rooms look bright and spacious. (iii) Decorative items and indoor plants, without blocking movement.
Suggest space-saving ideas for a one-room house (three points).

(i) Use a diwan, sofa-cum-bed and folding beds for sleeping. (ii) Use a folding dining or study table fixed on the wall and built-in storage. (iii) Mark and distinguish the cooking, sleeping and sitting areas by screens or furniture.
la: Explain the space management of the kitchen and bathroom, including kitchen layouts.

(i) Things used often are stored at a convenient height, heavy containers at floor level and rare items in dead storage. (ii) A utensil washing area should be near the cooking area. (iii) Layouts are one-walled, two-walled, L-shaped and U-shaped, in sitting or standing kitchens. (iv) A folding wall table saves space for dining. (v) A bathroom needs storage for toiletries, water supply, sloping non-slippery floor, and electric points away from water. (vi) A clothesline near the washing area avoids unnecessary movement.
